name: Doutai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: 3.1 STRESS — Stress, often manifested by length, is found on the first syllable of the word. As such, it is not emic.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim at McAllister & McAllister 1991:134 in the SIL PDF we hold (p. 21), and the Hartzler afterword caveat is verbatim at pp. 141-142. (2) Deciding source: a 1991 SIL field phonology article, the only description of Doutai in existence per Glottolog (1 descriptive ref) and the SIL archive (1 item for tds); Clouse 1997 (held) independently states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain and defers to McAllister for Doutai. No reference grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study was found in any bibliography opened; the language is moribund (~335 speakers in 1991). (3) list of works to obtain: empty — nothing unheld is known to exist. sources.quote: "3.1 STRESS — Stress, often manifested by length, is found on the first syllable of the word. As such, it is not emic." (p. 134). Supporting, editor's afterword p. 142: "A change in this position was forced when an across-the-board first syllable stress analysis was adopted. ... Further investigation, in fact, may well reveal factors which will either disprove the stress rule, or give clues to the assimilation of these apparently paradoxical factors."

sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-85), 133-236. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
sources.note: Section 11 'Tone typology' (p.152): tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and was most likely a feature of some protolanguages; all modern languages have at least high and low tone; Duvle and Sikaritai have only these (Martin 1991 analyses Sikaritai as pitch accent); Obokuitai has a fall; 'Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise'; four of Iau's eight tones 'correspond to the four tones found in the other Lakes Plain languages'. Secondhand for Doutai (author's fieldwork is Kirikiri); no TBU/domain/rule analysis.…
